channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Running Google’s Gemma on Satlyt’s orbital AI (w/ CEO Rama Afullo)
gist: Satlyt CEO Rama Afullo (rendered 'SAT lit'/'Rama Aulo' in the auto-transcript) explains his software for orchestrating AI workloads across heterogeneous satellites, including running Google's Gemma on board and filtering data so only ~11.7% needs costly downlink. He frames orbital compute economics around launch cost (Starship ~$1,000/kg vs ~$100/kg needed for parity vs $15,000/kg rideshare today), power, latency and thermals, and predicts 100,000 satellites in 3–5 years and direct-to-device satellites displacing telcos within ~10 years.

themes.theme: Orbital compute economics & launch cost curve

insights.claim: Rama Afullo says Starship launch costs are estimated at about $1,000 per kilogram to orbit, and orbital data centers need roughly $100 per kilogram to reach parity with terrestrial data centers.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: A ~10x further drop in launch cost is the gating variable for orbital data centers; track Starship cost/kg disclosures as the key milestone.
insights.quote: the estimation is that they're down to about $1,000 a kilogram

insights.claim: Typical satellite operators today pay about $15,000 per kilogram for rideshare launches, roughly 15x the Starship estimate, so most of the industry is far from the cost curve that makes orbital compute viable.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Cost advantage accrues to whoever owns heavy-lift capacity; small operators remain structurally disadvantaged until rideshare prices fall.
insights.quote: they're paying $15,000 a kilogram for ride share

insights.claim: Orbital compute reaching mass-market cost parity requires heavy-lift vehicles such as SpaceX Starship and Blue Origin's New Glenn to be in full operation, since larger payloads are needed to deploy satellites at scale.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Starship catch/reuse success and New Glenn cadence are leading indicators for the entire orbital data center thesis.
insights.quote: Starship needs to work, Blue Origin's New Glenn needs to work

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis frames the current cost of space-based compute as roughly 10x terrestrial clusters, and notes Elon Musk, Google and Starcloud are all pursuing orbital compute simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Orbital compute is becoming a crowded race among large incumbents; differentiation for startups will need to be in software/orchestration rather than hardware.
insights.quote: maybe 10 times more expensive to put it in space

insights.claim: Satlyt claims its orbital compute business is already cost effective because it does not build its own hardware, instead running software on other operators' satellites.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Asset-light software layers in space can monetize before launch costs fall, unlike hardware-heavy orbital data center plays.
insights.quote: for satellites it's already cost effective because we don't build our own hardware

insights.claim: Rama Afullo argues that community opposition to terrestrial data centers ('folks don't actually want data centers in their backyards') is one driver pushing compute into orbit.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Local permitting and NIMBY friction for data centers strengthens the long-term demand case for off-planet capacity.
insights.quote: folks don't actually want data centers in their backyards

insights.claim: Placing compute satellites in sun-synchronous orbit gives near-continuous solar access, addressing power, which Afullo calls probably the biggest limiting factor for compute generally.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: If power is the binding constraint on AI, orbital solar is a structural alternative to grid-constrained terrestrial build-outs.
insights.quote: power is probably the biggest limiting factor for compute in general

insights.claim: Total system latency is the single biggest metric in telecoms and space communication, and on-board edge processing in space is the base case for orbital compute (e.g., emergency and wildfire response).
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Edge compute on satellites is the near-term, already-needed use case; bigger AI training in orbit is the later extension.
insights.quote: biggest metric in sort of telecoms and space communication in general uh to measure whether or not we're doing things uh the right way is the total latency of the system

insights.claim: Because LEO satellites move at about 17,500 mph, an orbital data center can be positioned over any point on Earth within 90 minutes, unlike fixed-location cloud regions.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Mobile 'cloud regions' could matter for sovereignty, security redundancy, and rapid-response imaging markets.
insights.quote: you can have this data center wherever you want at any point on Earth within 90 minutes

insights.claim: There are about 20,000 satellites in space today, and Afullo predicts at least 100,000 within the next 3 to 5 years, though he says the amount of compute and relay capability matters more than satellite count.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: A 5x increase in satellites expands the addressable base for satellite software, orchestration and ground-station services.
insights.quote: It'll be at least at 100,000 in the next 3 to 5 years

insights.claim: Some orbital compute now being deployed is about 10x the total compute ever put across the roughly 20,000 satellites currently in space, and Afullo expects that to rise again within the next year.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: A step-change in orbital compute density signals that thermal and power solutions are becoming the next bottleneck and investment area.
insights.quote: some of the compute that's being set up now is like 10x the total compute ever put across these 20,000 satellites

insights.claim: Satlyt is building a Kubernetes-like orchestration layer for satellites, scheduling containerized workloads across heterogeneous satellites with dissimilar architectures, including container registry, telemetry analysis, compression, and encryption services.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Interoperability across satellite makers is an unsolved standards gap; an orchestration layer could become sticky infrastructure if it wins adoption.
insights.quote: what we attempting to do is to do this across heterogeneous systems

insights.claim: Satlyt has run Google's Gemma small language model on board satellites in orbit, and Google DeepMind published a case study on the work.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Validates small open models as viable for in-orbit inference; Google is positioning Gemma as an edge/space model.
insights.quote: we've chosen to use Google Gemma right as a small language model so running on the edge in space

insights.claim: In Satlyt's demo, on-board AI found that only 11.7% of a satellite's captured data was useful to downlink, while ground-station operators charge about $10 to $20 per gigabyte to bring data down.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: On-orbit filtering can cut downlink spend by most of the bill, a direct ROI pitch for satellite operators and a headwind for per-GB ground-station revenue.
insights.quote: you pay like $10 to $20 a gigabyte to the ground station operator

insights.claim: The demo constrained satellite workloads to a 15-watt power budget on an 8 GB, six-core Nvidia Jetson Nano-class onboard computer across five satellites.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Current in-orbit inference runs on tiny power envelopes, so near-term space AI is edge inference, not frontier training.

insights.claim: Satlyt is working with NASA (Glenn Research Center) on using delay-tolerant networking to relay 4K video from the Moon through lunar-orbit satellites to low Earth orbit and down to Earth with low latency, packet loss and bit-flip protection.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Government lunar programs provide early contract revenue for space networking software ahead of commercial demand.
insights.quote: part of what NASA is tasking us to do

themes.theme: Disruption of telcos, insurance and data advantages

insights.claim: Afullo predicts direct-to-cell and direct-to-device satellite services will essentially eradicate the typical ground-based telco within about 10 years, making them a relic like the landline.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: A long-dated bear thesis on terrestrial telco infrastructure and a bull case for direct-to-device satellite players.
insights.quote: it essentially eradicates the typical telco

insights.claim: Afullo says that during the Palisades fires in LA, insurers accessed satellite data on the fire outlook faster than the public, and some changed their policies just before the fires hit.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Faster space-derived data creates informational edges for insurers and traders; latency of Earth-observation data is monetizable.
insights.quote: a few of them changed their policies just before those fires hit

insights.claim: On the space heat debate, Afullo says both sides are right: space is cold, but in vacuum heat must be radiated away, so compute at scale needs massive radiators like those on the International Space Station.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Radiator mass and area are a real cost driver in orbital data center economics; thermal tech is a picks-and-shovels opportunity.
insights.quote: they're both correct, right?

insights.claim: Intel Starfire and Nvidia's Space One Vera Rubin module are space-specific compute modules designed to run hotter and at around 3,000 watts, effectively sidestepping the thermal debate by running chips harder.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Chipmakers are productizing space-grade AI compute; watch Nvidia and Intel space modules as a new segment.

insights.claim: Commodity hardware with moving parts survives launch: many Nvidia Jetson Nanos with spinning fans are operating in orbit, following Planet Labs' approach of ignoring conventional wisdom, though radiation hardening or shielding is needed for longevity.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Cheap COTS hardware lowers the barrier to orbital compute, but longevity requires costly shielding and testing.
insights.quote: we've got a lot of Nvidia Jess or Nanos in orbit and they have a spinning fan

insights.claim: Afullo expects the smartest space companies to pair with a terrestrial counterpart that applies orbital learnings and data on Earth, analogous to how space programs gave rise to microwaves and solar panels.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Look for space startups with terrestrial spinoff products or partners as a second revenue leg.
insights.quote: probably the smartest space players will make sure that they have a terrestrial

insights.claim: Afullo says that while at Google he pitched orbital compute and data centers but Google prioritized terrestrial LLM competition with ChatGPT, and at SpaceX he was told the last people who proposed orbital compute were no longer at the company, prompting him to leave and found Satlyt about two years ago.
insights.speaker: Rama Afullo (Satlyt CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly incumbents flipped on orbital compute; early contrarian founders may hold a timing advantage.
insights.quote: the last people who proposed something like this are no longer at the company
